lesson_plan.title: Build a Movie Tracking App
lesson_plan.description: A progressive lesson plan for building a multi-user movie tracking app with Next.js and Supabase. No prior coding experience required.

lessons.title: Project setup & first pages
lessons.subtitle: Create your movie tracking app from scratch, build two pages, and understand how they connect to each other.
lessons.goal: A running Next.js app with a home page showing placeholder movie cards and a detail page for each movie. Clicking a card takes you to that movie's page. Nothing is real data yet — that comes later. The structure is in place.

foundational_reading.title: What it means to build something
foundational_reading.reason: Sets the right mindset — you're directing, not coding.

foundational_reading.title: You're the architect, AI is the contractor
foundational_reading.reason: Explains your relationship with Cursor before you use it.

foundational_reading.title: What happens when you type a URL
foundational_reading.reason: Understand what running locally means before you do it.

foundational_reading.title: What a component is
foundational_reading.reason: You'll be building components immediately — know what they are first.

steps.title: Install Cursor and create your project
steps.content: If you don't have Cursor installed, download it at cursor.com and open it. This is the tool you'll use for everything — it's like a code editor, but AI can read and write your code alongside you. Open Cursor's terminal (View → Terminal, or press Ctrl+backtick) and run this to create your project. When it asks questions: Tailwind → Yes, App Router → Yes, everything else → default. Then navigate into it.

inline_articles.note: Read this now — it explains what Cursor is and how it differs from a regular code editor.

steps.title: Run the app for the first time
steps.content: Before you change anything, make sure the default app runs. Open Cursor's built-in browser (View → Browser) and go to localhost:3000. You should see the default Next.js welcome page. This means your app is running locally on your machine — nobody else can see it yet.

inline_articles.note: It explains the difference between a static and dynamic site, and what running locally actually means.

steps.title: Build the home page — movie card grid
steps.content: Now you'll ask Cursor to build your first real page. Open the chat panel and describe what you want. Before prompting, read CURSOR-102 so you understand how the chat panel works. The goal is a home page with a grid of movie cards — each showing a title, year, and placeholder poster. The data is hardcoded for now.
steps.prompt_guidance: Describe the page layout, what each card shows, that data should be hardcoded as an array, and that you want Tailwind for styling. Be specific about columns and what appears on each card.
steps.example_prompt: Build a home page at app/page.tsx for a movie tracking app. Create a responsive grid of movie cards using Tailwind CSS — 2 columns on mobile, 4 on desktop. Each card should show a gray rectangle as a poster placeholder, the movie title, and the release year. Hardcode an array of 8 placeholder movies with title and year fields. Cards should be clean and minimal with rounded corners and a subtle border.
steps.browser_check: After Cursor applies its changes, look at localhost:3000 in the built-in browser. You should see a grid of movie cards. If something looks off — cards are the wrong size, the layout is broken, text is missing — describe exactly what you see back to Cursor and ask it to fix it. You don't need to understand the code. Describe the visual problem.

inline_articles.note: Read before prompting — it explains how the chat panel works.
Read after this step — it explains props, which is how your movie data is being passed into each card.

steps.title: Build the movie detail page
steps.content: Now you'll add a second page — a detail view for each movie. Before prompting, read COMP-205 to understand how Next.js handles routing and what a dynamic route is.
steps.prompt_guidance: Tell Cursor you want a dynamic route for movie detail pages, that clicking a card should navigate there, what should appear on the detail page, and that it should reuse the same hardcoded movies array from the home page.
steps.example_prompt: Add a dynamic movie detail page at app/movies/[id]/page.tsx. Add a unique id field to each movie in the hardcoded array. Clicking a movie card on the home page should navigate to /movies/[id]. The detail page should show the movie title, year, a larger poster placeholder, and a short placeholder description. Import the movies array from a shared file so both pages use the same data.
steps.browser_check: Click a movie card on the home page. You should land on a detail page showing that movie's title. Then use the back button and click a different card — it should show a different title. If clicking a card does nothing, or you land on an error page, paste what you see back into Cursor and ask it to fix the routing.

inline_articles.note: Read before prompting — it explains how Next.js dynamic routing works and why the [id] in the filename matters.

steps.title: Add a navigation header
steps.content: A navigation bar that lives across all pages will make this feel like a real app. In Next.js this goes in the root layout file so it renders on every page automatically.
steps.prompt_guidance: Ask for a simple header component with the app name and a home link, added to the root layout. Describe the style — minimal, with a bottom border.
steps.example_prompt: Add a simple navigation header to app/layout.tsx. It should show the app name "MovieTracker" on the left and a link back to the home page on the right. Style it with Tailwind — clean and minimal with a bottom border. It should appear on every page automatically.
steps.browser_check: The header should now appear on both the home page and the detail page. Click the home link from a detail page — it should take you back to the movie grid. If the header only shows on one page or the link doesn't work, describe that to Cursor.

inline_articles.note: Read if anything about the structure Cursor wrote looks unfamiliar.
Read if anything about the styling Cursor wrote looks unfamiliar.

steps.title: Polish — fix anything that looks off
steps.content: Before you wrap this lesson, spend a few minutes looking at the app as a user would. Use Cursor's browser and resize the window between mobile and desktop width. Look at both pages. Anything that bothers you visually — describe it to Cursor in plain language and ask it to fix it. This is the loop you'll use constantly: look at the page, describe what's wrong, let Cursor fix it.
steps.prompt_guidance: Describe what you see, what you expected instead, and where on the page the issue is. You don't need technical terms. "The movie cards on mobile are stacked in one column and feel too narrow — I want them to feel more like a proper grid" is a perfect prompt.

steps.title: Write your first acceptance criteria
steps.content: You've just built something that works end-to-end. Before you move on, let's introduce a concept that will make every future lesson go smoother: acceptance criteria. Before you build a feature, you write down what done looks like. Then after you build it, you check each item. If something fails, you go back and fix it. This is how professional teams ship software — and it's how you should prompt Cursor when features get more complex. The most common way to write acceptance criteria is as a user story — a one-sentence description of who wants something, what they want, and why. Go check each acceptance criteria item in Cursor's browser. If any fail, fix them before moving on.

inline_articles.note: Goes deeper on acceptance criteria and why defining done before you build leads to better features and better prompts.

concept.title: Acceptance criteria & user stories
concept.body: Acceptance criteria is a plain-language list of conditions that define when something is finished — not 'I think it looks okay' but a specific checklist you can verify by actually using the thing you built. The most common way to write it is as a user story: As a [user], I want to [action], so that [reason]. Under each story, you write the specific checkboxes that define when it's satisfied.

user_story_example.i_want_to: see a grid of movies on the home page
user_story_example.so_that: I can browse what's available and find something to watch

acceptance_criteria: Home page shows a grid of movie cards with a title and year on each
Grid is 2 columns on mobile and 4 columns on desktop
Clicking a card navigates to that movie's detail page
Detail page shows the correct title for the movie that was clicked
Navigation header appears on both pages
Clicking the home link in the header returns to the movie grid
lessons.completion_note: The data is hardcoded — that's intentional. Next lesson you'll make the app look polished and work properly across screen sizes.

lessons.title: Layout, styling & responsiveness
lessons.subtitle: Make the app look good and work across screen sizes. You'll go from a rough structure to something that actually feels like a real product.
lessons.goal: A polished movie card grid that looks good on mobile and desktop. A properly laid out detail page. A consistent visual language — spacing, typography, and color that feel intentional.

foundational_reading.title: The box model
foundational_reading.reason: Everything on a page is a box. Understanding this makes spacing make sense.

foundational_reading.title: What responsive design is
foundational_reading.reason: Why building for multiple screen sizes matters and how it works conceptually.

foundational_reading.title: Tailwind CSS
foundational_reading.reason: You've already used it — now understand what utility-first styling actually means.

steps.title: Audit what you have
steps.content: Before prompting anything new, open Cursor's browser and look at your app with fresh eyes. Resize the window to about 375px wide — mobile width. Ask yourself: does this look like something you'd actually use? What feels off? Make a short mental list of what bothers you — cramped cards, inconsistent spacing, fonts that feel too big or too small. You're about to fix all of it. This step is just about seeing it clearly first.

inline_articles.note: It explains breakpoints, which is the mechanism behind how layouts shift at different screen widths.

steps.title: Improve the movie card design
steps.content: Your cards from lesson 1 were functional but probably not beautiful. Make them feel like a real app — portrait poster on top, title and year below, a subtle hover effect.
steps.prompt_guidance: Describe the poster aspect ratio, how title and year sit below it, font sizes, spacing, border radius, and any hover state.
steps.example_prompt: Improve the movie card component. The poster placeholder should be a 2:3 aspect ratio rectangle — portrait, like a real movie poster — with the movie's posterColor as background. Below it, show the movie title in medium weight and the year in a smaller muted color. Add a subtle hover effect — slightly lift the card or change the border color. Keep it clean, no heavy shadows.
steps.browser_check: Cards should look noticeably better. Poster is portrait, text sits cleanly below, hovering gives feedback. If proportions feel wrong — "the poster feels too short and wide" — describe it to Cursor.

inline_articles.note: It covers design tokens and CSS variables, how consistent spacing and color get applied across components.

steps.title: Fix the grid layout and spacing
steps.content: Look at the overall page. Is there breathing room? Does it feel crammed or floating in space? This step is about the container — not the cards themselves.
steps.prompt_guidance: Describe the max width, page padding, gap between cards, column count at different sizes, and any heading above the grid.
steps.example_prompt: Improve the home page layout. The movie grid should have a max width of around 1200px and be centered. Add comfortable padding so content never touches screen edges on mobile. Gap between cards should feel generous. Add a page heading "All Movies" above the grid in a clean medium-weight font.
steps.browser_check: Resize from mobile to desktop. Grid should reflow smoothly — 2 columns narrow, 4 wide. Content should never touch screen edges. There should be a clear heading above the grid.

inline_articles.note: Flexbox controls your layout — understanding it helps you describe problems accurately.
Grid controls your layout — understanding it helps you describe problems accurately.

steps.title: Style the detail page
steps.content: The detail page is probably just stacked text right now. Give it a proper layout — large poster left, info right on desktop, stacked on mobile.
steps.prompt_guidance: Describe the two-column desktop layout, how they stack on mobile, what info appears on the right, font sizes, and spacing.
steps.example_prompt: Redesign the movie detail page. On desktop: large portrait poster on the left (about 1/3 width) and movie info on the right — title large, year muted below, description below that. On mobile: stack vertically with poster on top. Add a back link above the layout. Keep max width consistent with the home page.
steps.browser_check: At desktop: poster left, info right. Narrow the window: they stack. Back link visible and works.

steps.title: Polish the navigation header
steps.content: Make the nav feel finished — consistent height, clean typography, proper spacing that aligns with the rest of the page.
steps.example_prompt: Polish the navigation header. Give it a fixed height with comfortable vertical padding. Style "MovieTracker" with slightly bolder weight. Make the home link look like a proper nav link with a hover state. The header should align to the same max width and padding as the page content below it.
steps.browser_check: The nav should feel visually connected to the page — not floating separately. Check on both mobile and desktop.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria
steps.content: Before moving on, walk through the app and verify each acceptance criteria item. If anything fails, go back and fix it.

acceptance_criteria: Movie cards have a portrait poster placeholder with title and year below
Cards have a visible hover state
Home page grid has max width, is centered, has comfortable padding
Grid is 2 columns on mobile and 4 on desktop
Detail page shows poster left, info right on desktop — stacked on mobile
Navigation header is polished and consistent across pages
No content touches screen edges on mobile
lessons.completion_note: Next lesson you'll replace the hardcoded array with real data from a JSON file and wire up dynamic routing properly.

lessons.title: Data piping & routing with JSON
lessons.subtitle: Replace hardcoded content with real data loaded from a file. This is your first taste of how data flows through an app.
lessons.goal: Movie data lives in a single JSON file. Both the home page and detail pages pull from it. Adding or removing a movie from the file immediately changes what appears in the app — no code changes needed.

foundational_reading.title: What is data
foundational_reading.reason: The concept of stored information before you start moving it around.

foundational_reading.title: Data formats
foundational_reading.reason: JSON is what you're about to use — understand what it is first.

foundational_reading.title: Arrays and objects
foundational_reading.reason: Your movie list is an array of objects. This explains what that means.

steps.title: Create the movies data file
steps.content: Right now your movie data is scattered inside component files. Pull it into one central JSON file — any part of the app that needs movie data will read from here.
steps.example_prompt: Create a data file at lib/movies.json. Each movie should have: id (a unique slug like "the-godfather"), title, year, description (2–3 sentences), genre (array of strings), and posterColor (a hex color for the poster placeholder background). Populate it with 12 realistic movies across different genres. This will be the single source of truth for all movie data.

inline_articles.note: It explains functions and imports, which is how other files will access this data file.

steps.title: Wire the home page to the data file
steps.content: Replace the hardcoded array in your home page with an import from the data file. The page should look identical — but data now flows from one central place.
steps.example_prompt: Update app/page.tsx to import movie data from lib/movies.json instead of a hardcoded array. Remove the hardcoded movies from the component. Use each movie's posterColor field as the background color of the poster placeholder. Everything else should look the same.
steps.browser_check: The home page should show 12 movies with colored poster placeholders. Open movies.json and change a movie's title — save it and the page should update. That's data flowing through your app.

steps.title: Wire the detail page to the data file
steps.content: The detail page needs to find the right movie based on the URL. When you visit /movies/the-godfather it should look that movie up in the JSON and display its data.
steps.example_prompt: Update the movie detail page at app/movies/[id]/page.tsx to look up the movie from lib/movies.json using the id URL parameter. Display the real title, year, description, and use posterColor for the poster background. If no movie with that id exists, show a "Movie not found" message with a link back home.
steps.browser_check: Click several different cards — each detail page should show that specific movie's real data. Visit /movies/fake-id — you should see the not-found message.

inline_articles.note: It explains how Next.js dynamic routing works and why the [id] in the filename matters.

steps.title: Test the data flow
steps.content: The whole point of a data file is that changing data in one place changes it everywhere. Open movies.json and make a few changes: rename a movie, change a year, add a completely new entry. Save after each change and check your browser. This is a big conceptual moment — you've separated your data from your presentation. The component doesn't care what the data says, it just displays whatever it receives. That's a pattern you'll use for the rest of the course.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria
steps.content: Before moving on, verify each acceptance criteria item in Cursor's browser.

acceptance_criteria: Movie data lives in a single lib/movies.json file
Home page imports from that file — no hardcoded arrays in components
Each card shows the real title, year, and colored poster placeholder
Clicking a card loads that movie's real data on the detail page
Visiting /movies/fake-id shows a not-found message
Adding a new movie to movies.json makes it appear on the home page without code changes
lessons.completion_note: Next lesson you'll add interactivity — a dark mode toggle and a watchlist you can add movies to.

lessons.title: Local state & UI interactions
lessons.subtitle: Make the app interactive. You'll add a dark mode toggle and a watchlist — your first experience with state, which is data that changes while the app is running.
lessons.goal: A working dark mode toggle that persists between page loads. An Add to watchlist button on each movie. A /watchlist page showing movies you've added. State resets on full browser refresh — that's expected and intentional at this stage.

foundational_reading.title: State: data that changes over time
foundational_reading.reason: The core concept behind everything interactive in this lesson.

foundational_reading.title: Events and interactivity
foundational_reading.reason: How user actions like clicks trigger things to happen.

foundational_reading.title: React hooks: the concept
foundational_reading.reason: useState is what you'll use — understand what it does before Cursor writes it.

steps.title: Add a dark mode toggle
steps.content: Dark mode is a good first state exercise because it's binary — on or off — and you can see it working immediately. Tailwind has built-in dark mode support which makes this straightforward.
steps.example_prompt: Add a dark mode toggle to the navigation header. Use Tailwind's dark mode class strategy. Store the preference in localStorage so it persists on page refresh. The toggle should be a simple button — a sun/moon icon or just "Light / Dark" text. When dark mode is on, the page background, cards, and text should all switch to dark variants using Tailwind dark: classes.
steps.browser_check: Toggle dark mode on and off — the whole page should switch. Refresh — the preference should persist. If it resets on refresh, describe that to Cursor and ask it to fix the localStorage implementation.

inline_articles.note: It explains asynchronous code, which touches on how localStorage reads and writes work.

steps.title: Add Add to watchlist button
steps.content: Add a button to each movie card that adds it to a watchlist. The watchlist lives in React state for now — it exists while the page is open, but resets on refresh. Persisting it to a database comes in lesson 7.
steps.example_prompt: Add watchlist functionality. Create a watchlist state that holds an array of movie ids. On each movie card, add a small button — "Add to watchlist" if not added, "Remove" if it is. The button should visually indicate the current state. The watchlist state should live high enough in the component tree to be passed to a watchlist page. For now, log the watchlist array to the console when it changes.
steps.browser_check: Click Add to watchlist on several movies. The button should visually change to Remove. Open the browser console (right-click → Inspect → Console) and verify the array updates. Refresh — it resets. That's expected.

steps.title: Build the watchlist page
steps.content: Create a /watchlist page that shows only the movies you've added, reusing the same card design from the home page.
steps.example_prompt: Create a watchlist page at app/watchlist/page.tsx. It should display only movies added to the watchlist using the same MovieCard component. If the watchlist is empty, show "No movies added yet" with a link to browse. Add a "Watchlist" link to the navigation header. Pass the watchlist state down so the page can access it.
steps.browser_check: Add a few movies then navigate to /watchlist — those movies should appear. Remove one from the home page — it should disappear from the watchlist. Visit /watchlist with nothing added — empty state should show.

inline_articles.note: It explains context and global state, the more scalable version of what you're doing right now with prop passing.

steps.title: State vs. persistence
steps.content: Your watchlist works, but refreshing loses everything. That's because it lives in React state — memory that exists only while the page is open. Dark mode persists because you saved it to localStorage, which survives refreshes. Neither is a real database. A database persists data permanently, across devices, and for multiple users. That's what you'll add in lesson 6.

concept.title: State vs. persistence
concept.body: State is temporary — it lives in memory while the page is open. localStorage is local-only — it survives refreshes but only on your device. A database is permanent and shared — it persists across devices and for multiple users. Each layer has its place.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria
steps.content: Before moving on, verify each acceptance criteria item in Cursor's browser.

acceptance_criteria: Dark mode toggle switches the full page between light and dark
Dark mode preference persists on page refresh
Each movie card has an Add/Remove watchlist button that reflects current state
/watchlist page shows only added movies using the same card layout
Removing a movie on the home page removes it from the watchlist
Empty watchlist shows a helpful message and link to browse
Watchlist resets on refresh — this is expected at this stage
lessons.completion_note: Next lesson you'll sharpen your Cursor prompting skills before tackling the database.

lessons.title: Prompting & working with Cursor effectively
lessons.subtitle: Before you tackle the database, pause to sharpen your most important tool: how you communicate with Cursor. Better prompts mean better results, less back-and-forth, and fewer broken things.
lessons.goal: A .cursorrules file set up for your project. One existing component refactored using Cursor Agent. A clearer mental model for how to prompt effectively — context, specificity, and iteration.

foundational_reading.title: What prompting is
foundational_reading.reason: The foundational framing before you apply any techniques.

foundational_reading.title: The anatomy of a good prompt
foundational_reading.reason: Role, context, task, format, constraints — the five pieces.

foundational_reading.title: Being specific vs. being vague
foundational_reading.reason: Why specificity gets better results.

foundational_reading.title: Agent mode
foundational_reading.reason: You'll use this to let Cursor take multi-step actions in this lesson.

steps.title: Set up your .cursorrules file
steps.content: A .cursorrules file is a plain text file that sits in the root of your project. Cursor reads it automatically and uses it as permanent context for every prompt. Think of it as telling Cursor everything it needs to know about this project before it touches anything.
steps.example_prompt: Create a .cursorrules file for this project. It's a movie tracking app built with Next.js App Router and Tailwind CSS. We use a lib/movies.json file as the data source for now, moving to Supabase later. Always use Tailwind for styling — never write raw CSS. Components should be clean and minimal. Never hardcode data inside components. When making changes, only touch the files relevant to the task — don't refactor unrelated things.

inline_articles.note: It explains what .cursorrules does and how to get the most out of it.

steps.title: Compare a vague prompt vs. a specific one
steps.content: This is a practical exercise to feel the difference between a weak prompt and a strong one. You'll prompt Cursor twice for the same task — once vaguely, once with precision. First try the vague prompt: "Make the movie cards better." Look at what Cursor does — it'll probably make choices you didn't ask for. Undo those changes, then try the specific prompt below.
steps.example_prompt: Update the MovieCard component to show a genre badge in the top-left corner of the poster placeholder. Use the first genre in the genre array. The badge should be a small pill with a semi-transparent dark background and white text. Don't change anything else about the card design.
steps.browser_check: The specific prompt should produce exactly what you described — a genre badge, nothing else changed. The vague prompt probably changed things you didn't ask for. This is the core lesson: specificity gives you control.

steps.title: Use Agent mode to refactor a component
steps.content: Agent mode lets Cursor take multiple steps on its own — reading files, making changes across several files, and checking its own work. You'll use it to extract the movie card into a properly structured standalone component file.
steps.prompt_guidance: Give Agent clear instructions about where to find the current card code, where to move it, what the component should be called, and what it should accept as props. Tell it not to change the visual design.
steps.example_prompt: Use Agent mode: Extract the movie card UI into a standalone component at components/MovieCard.tsx. It should accept a movie object as a prop with title, year, posterColor, genre, and id fields. Import and use it in app/page.tsx. Don't change any styling or behavior — just move the code into a clean, reusable component structure.
steps.browser_check: The home page should look identical. Open app/page.tsx — it should be noticeably shorter, importing MovieCard rather than defining it inline. If the page breaks, paste the error to Cursor and ask it to fix it.

inline_articles.note: Reviewing changes is a critical skill when using Agent mode.
Debugging is a critical skill when using Agent mode.

steps.title: Practice the iteration loop
steps.content: Pick one thing about your app that still bothers you visually and iterate on it using at least 3 rounds of prompting — each one more specific than the last. Practice describing visual problems precisely.

concept.title: Prompting is a loop, not a one-shot
concept.body: The best AI-assisted builders don't expect a perfect result on the first prompt. They treat it like a conversation: prompt → check the result → refine → check again. Each round gets closer to what they actually want. The key is being specific about what's wrong in your follow-up. 'That's not right' is useless. 'The badge is overlapping the movie title — it should be inside the poster area, not below it' gives Cursor exactly what it needs to fix it.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria
steps.content: Before moving on, verify each acceptance criteria item.

acceptance_criteria: .cursorrules file exists in the project root with meaningful project context
MovieCard exists as a standalone component in a components/ folder
Home page imports MovieCard rather than defining it inline
Genre badge appears on each card
App looks and functions identically to before this lesson
lessons.completion_note: Next lesson you'll connect a real database — replacing the JSON file with Supabase.

lessons.title: Supabase setup & first table
lessons.subtitle: Connect the app to a real database. This is one of the biggest conceptual leaps in the course — moving from local files to persistent, cloud-hosted data.
lessons.goal: A Supabase project with a movies table. The app fetches movie data from Supabase instead of the JSON file. Adding a row in Supabase appears in the app without touching code.

foundational_reading.title: What a database is
foundational_reading.reason: The conceptual leap from a file to a real database before you touch Supabase.

foundational_reading.title: Rows, columns, and tables
foundational_reading.reason: The basic unit of what you're about to create.

foundational_reading.title: Environment variables
foundational_reading.reason: Your Supabase keys live here — understand why before you add them.

foundational_reading.title: What Supabase is
foundational_reading.reason: The overview before you create your account.

steps.title: Create a Supabase project
steps.content: Go to supabase.com and create a free account. Create a new project — name it movie-tracker and choose a region close to you. The database password it generates is important — save it somewhere safe. Once the project is created, take a minute to look around the dashboard. The Table Editor, SQL Editor, and Authentication tabs are the three things you'll use most in this course.

inline_articles.note: It walks through the Supabase dashboard so you know what you're looking at.

steps.title: Create the movies table
steps.content: In the Supabase Table Editor, create a new table called movies. Ask Cursor to help you design the schema before you create it in Supabase. Then create the columns in the Table Editor. Once the table exists, manually add 3–4 movies using the UI to confirm it works.
steps.example_prompt: I'm creating a movies table in Supabase. Based on the current lib/movies.json structure, what columns should I create and what data types should they be? I want to match the existing data shape as closely as possible.

inline_articles.note: It covers creating your first table in Supabase's UI.

steps.title: Connect your app to Supabase
steps.content: Install the Supabase client and add your connection keys as environment variables. Go to your Supabase project → Settings → API to find your project URL and anon key. Create a .env.local file in your project root — this is where your secrets live. Never commit this file to GitHub.
steps.example_prompt: Set up Supabase in this Next.js project. Install the client, create a lib/supabase.ts file that initializes the Supabase client using NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_URL and NEXT_PUBLIC_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY environment variables. Create a .env.local file with placeholder values and add it to .gitignore if it isn't already.

inline_articles.note: It explains why secrets in environment variables matter and what happens when they leak.

steps.title: Replace the JSON file with a Supabase query
steps.content: Update the home page to fetch movies from Supabase instead of importing from the JSON file.
steps.example_prompt: Update app/page.tsx to fetch movies from Supabase instead of importing from lib/movies.json. Use the Supabase client from lib/supabase.ts to query the movies table and return all rows. This is a Next.js server component so you can use async/await directly. Handle the case where the fetch fails by showing an error message. Keep the same MovieCard component and layout.
steps.browser_check: The home page should show the movies you manually added in Supabase. Go to the Table Editor and add another row — refresh your app and it should appear. If you see an empty page or error, paste it to Cursor.

steps.title: Populate the table from the JSON file
steps.content: Manually adding 12 movies in Supabase's UI is tedious. Ask Cursor to write a quick script to import your existing JSON data into the table.
steps.example_prompt: Write a one-time Node.js script at scripts/seed.js that reads from lib/movies.json and inserts all movies into the Supabase movies table using the Supabase client. Log success or failure for each insert. I'll run it once manually.
steps.browser_check: Check the Supabase Table Editor to confirm all 12 movies are there. Reload your app — the full list should appear.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria
steps.content: Before moving on, verify each acceptance criteria item.

acceptance_criteria: Supabase project exists with a movies table matching the data shape
App fetches movies from Supabase — not from the JSON file
All 12 movies appear on the home page
Adding a row in Supabase dashboard makes it appear in the app on refresh
Supabase keys are in .env.local and not committed to the repo
Detail pages still work — each movie loads its own data

lessons.title: CRUD — adding & managing movies
lessons.subtitle: Let users create, update, and delete movies from within the app. This is the first time your users will be able to change data — and the first time a mistake could break something permanently.
lessons.goal: An Add movie form that writes to Supabase. An edit button on the detail page. A delete option with confirmation. All changes persist on refresh.

foundational_reading.title: CRUD operations
foundational_reading.reason: Create, Read, Update, Delete — the four things you're about to build.

foundational_reading.title: Queries: asking questions of your data
foundational_reading.reason: You've been reading data — now you'll write it too.

foundational_reading.title: What a promise is
foundational_reading.reason: Writing to a database is async — this explains the mental model.

steps.title: Build the add movie form
steps.content: Create a form at /movies/new that lets a user fill in movie details and submit them to Supabase. On success it should redirect to the home page where the new movie appears.
steps.example_prompt: Create an "Add Movie" page at app/movies/new/page.tsx. It should be a form with fields for title, year, description, genre (comma-separated), and posterColor (a hex color input). On submit, insert the movie into the Supabase movies table. On success, redirect to the home page. On error, show an inline error message. Add an "Add Movie" button to the navigation header that links to this page.
steps.browser_check: Fill in the form and submit. Navigate to the home page — the new movie should appear. Check the Supabase Table Editor — the row should be there.

steps.title: Add edit functionality
steps.content: From the movie detail page, a user should be able to edit the movie's details. The easiest pattern is an edit page that pre-fills the form with existing data.
steps.example_prompt: Add an "Edit" button to the movie detail page that navigates to app/movies/[id]/edit/page.tsx. The edit page should be a form pre-filled with the current movie's data. On submit, update the existing row in Supabase using the movie's id. On success, redirect back to the movie detail page. Only show the Edit button for now — we'll add auth later to restrict who can edit.
steps.browser_check: Click Edit on any movie. The form should pre-fill with that movie's current data. Change the title and save — the detail page should show the updated title. Confirm the change in Supabase.

steps.title: Add delete functionality
steps.content: Deleting is permanent. Make sure there's a confirmation step so users can't accidentally delete things.
steps.example_prompt: Add a Delete button to the movie detail page. When clicked, show a confirmation dialog — "Are you sure you want to delete this movie? This cannot be undone." If confirmed, delete the row from Supabase and redirect to the home page. If cancelled, do nothing.
steps.browser_check: Click Delete on a movie. Confirmation dialog appears. Cancel — nothing happens. Confirm — the movie is gone from the home page and from Supabase. Add it back using the Add Movie form to verify that still works.

steps.title: Optimistic UI — making the app feel fast
steps.content: Right now when you delete a movie, the UI waits for Supabase to confirm before updating. On a slow connection it feels sluggish. Optimistic UI means updating the UI immediately, assuming success, and rolling back if something goes wrong.
steps.example_prompt: Update the delete flow to be optimistic. When the user confirms deletion, immediately remove the movie from the UI without waiting for Supabase to respond. If the Supabase delete fails, show an error and restore the movie in the UI. This should make deletion feel instant.

inline_articles.note: It covers perceived performance patterns including optimistic UI, skeleton screens, and lazy loading.

concept.title: What is optimistic UI?
concept.body: Optimistic UI means updating the interface immediately when a user takes an action, assuming it will succeed, rather than waiting for the server to confirm. If the server fails, you roll back. You've seen this in apps you use — when you like a post, the count goes up instantly before the server confirms. That's optimistic UI.

steps.title: Acceptance criteria
steps.content: Before moving on, verify each acceptance criteria item.

acceptance_criteria: Add Movie form creates a new row in Supabase and it appears on the home page
Edit form pre-fills with existing data and saves changes to Supabase
Delete requires confirmation and permanently removes the row
Deletion is optimistic — UI updates immediately
All changes persist on page refresh
Error states are handled — failed operations show a message, don't silently fail
